title: Freelance Change Request Kit
description: Stop doing extra work for free without arguing with clients. Fill-in revision policy for proposals (three strictness levels), a revision-or-change test with 12 examples, a change request form with a worked example, a two-minute pricing method, a feedback consolidation process, ten ready-to-send emails, and a change log and revision tracker. For designers, developers, writers and other project freelancers.

files.README.md:
# Freelance Change Request Kit

"Can you just add one more thing?" is how a profitable project turns into an unpaid one. This kit gives you a simple, friendly system for handling revisions and changes: you set the rules before work starts, you log every change as it comes in, you price it in two minutes, and you get a written yes before you do the extra work.

It works for any project-based freelancer: designers, developers, writers, editors, illustrators, video editors, consultants.

## The system in one paragraph

Your proposal says how many **revision rounds** are included and what counts as a revision versus a **change**. During the project you ask the client for **consolidated feedback** (one list per round, from one person). Anything that's a revision, you just do. Anything that's a change gets a short **change request**: what's being added, what it costs, how it moves the deadline. The client approves it in writing, you log it in the **change log**, and you add it to the next invoice. No arguments, no surprise bills, no silent unpaid work.

## What's inside

| File | What it's for |
|---|---|
| `revision-policy.md` | Fill-in policy text for your proposals, with three versions (light, standard, strict) |
| `revision-or-change.md` | A two-minute test to decide whether a request is a revision or a change, with 12 examples |
| `change-request-form.md` | A one-page change request you can paste into an email or doc, with a worked example |
| `pricing-a-change.md` | How to price a change fast, including the hidden costs most people forget |
| `feedback-consolidation.md` | How to get one clear feedback list per round instead of 40 scattered comments |
| `email-scripts.md` | Ten ready-to-send emails for the awkward moments |
| `change-log.csv` | Track every change request, its price, status and invoice, with example rows |
| `revision-tracker.csv` | Track rounds used per deliverable so you know when you've hit the limit |

## Setup (about 45 minutes, once)

1. **Policy (20 min):** pick a version in `revision-policy.md`, fill in the blanks and paste it into your proposal or project agreement template.
2. **Prices (15 min):** fill in your numbers in `pricing-a-change.md` (hourly rate, minimum change fee, rush multiplier).
3. **Templates (10 min):** copy `change-request-form.md` and `email-scripts.md` into wherever you keep reusable text (a notes app, text expander, email templates).

## On every project

1. At kickoff, remind the client how rounds work (Script 1 in `email-scripts.md`).
2. Start a fresh `revision-tracker.csv` and `change-log.csv` (or a tab per project).
3. When a request arrives, run the test in `revision-or-change.md`.
4. Revision: do it, tick the round. Change: send a change request, wait for a written yes, log it.
5. When you invoice, add every approved change from the log.

## A note on contracts

This kit gives you plain-language policy text and process, not legal advice. If you use a formal contract, make sure the revision and change wording in it matches what you tell the client, and get advice from a qualified professional where you live if you need a contract reviewed.
files.revision-policy.md:
# Revision and Change Policy

Paste one of these into your proposal, quote or project agreement. Replace everything in [brackets]. Then say the same thing out loud at kickoff: a policy only works if the client has actually read it.

## Before you choose: three decisions

1. **How many rounds?** Two rounds suit most design, writing and editing work. One round suits small, well-defined jobs. Three rounds suit brand identity or anything with many stakeholders. More than three usually means the brief wasn't clear; fix the brief instead.
2. **What happens after the rounds run out?** Extra rounds are billed at a fixed price per round or at your hourly rate. A fixed price per round is easier for clients to say yes to.
3. **How fast do you turn revisions around, and how fast must the client reply?** If the client takes three weeks to send feedback, your schedule slides. Say so in advance.

---

## Version A: Light (small jobs, friendly repeat clients)

> **Revisions.** This project includes [two] rounds of revisions. A round is one consolidated set of feedback sent in a single message. I'll return each round within [3] working days.
>
> **Changes.** Anything outside the agreed scope (new pages, new deliverables, a new direction) is a change. I'll send a short quote for any change before starting it, so there are never surprise costs.

## Version B: Standard (most projects)

> **What's included.** This project includes [two] rounds of revisions on each deliverable listed in the scope above.
>
> **What counts as a round.** A round is one consolidated list of feedback, sent in one message by [the project lead / named contact]. Feedback that arrives after I've started working on a round is added to the next round.
>
> **Revision vs. change.** A revision adjusts work that's already in scope: wording, colours, layout, fixing anything that doesn't match the brief. A change adds something new or reverses an approved decision: new pages, sections, features or formats, a new direction, or redoing work that was already approved.
>
> **How changes work.** For any change, I'll send a short change request with the cost and any effect on the timeline. Work on the change starts once you approve it in writing (a reply to the email is fine). Approved changes are added to the next invoice.
>
> **Extra rounds.** Additional revision rounds are [$X] per round per deliverable.
>
> **Timing.** I return each round within [3] working days. If feedback takes longer than [5] working days to arrive, the delivery date moves by the same amount, and I'll confirm the new date in writing.

## Version C: Strict (large projects, many stakeholders, past scope problems)

> Everything in Version B, plus:
>
> **One voice.** All feedback comes through [named contact], who is responsible for resolving disagreements between reviewers before sending it to me.
>
> **Approval is final.** When a deliverable is approved, later changes to it are treated as changes, not revisions, even if they're small.
>
> **Rush changes.** Changes requested with less than [3] working days' notice before a deadline are billed at [1.5x] the normal rate, if I'm able to accommodate them.
>
> **Minimum.** Each change request has a minimum fee of [$X], which covers the time to assess, quote and schedule it.

---

## Worked example (Version B, filled in)

A freelance designer, Sam, is quoting a five-page website design for a dental clinic.

> **What's included.** This project includes two rounds of revisions on each deliverable listed in the scope above (homepage design, four inner page designs, mobile versions).
>
> **What counts as a round.** A round is one consolidated list of feedback, sent in one message by Dr. Patel. Feedback that arrives after I've started working on a round is added to the next round.
>
> **Revision vs. change.** ... (unchanged)
>
> **Extra rounds.** Additional revision rounds are $180 per round per page.
>
> **Timing.** I return each round within 3 working days. If feedback takes longer than 5 working days to arrive, the delivery date moves by the same amount, and I'll confirm the new date in writing.

Why $180: Sam's rate is $90/hour and a typical round on one page takes about 2 hours.

## Saying it at kickoff

Policies are easy to skim past. Thirty seconds in the kickoff call prevents most disputes:

> "Quick note on how feedback works, so nothing's a surprise. You get two rounds on each page. A round is one list from Dr. Patel, so the team's comments get combined first. If something comes up that's new, not a tweak, I'll send a quick quote before doing it, so you're always in control of the budget. Sound good?"
files.revision-or-change.md:
# Revision or Change? The Two-Minute Test

When a request comes in, answer these four questions in order. Stop at the first "yes".

| # | Question | If yes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Does it fix something that doesn't match the brief, or an error on your side? | **Revision** (free, and doesn't use up a round if it's your mistake) |
| 2 | Does it add something new: a page, section, feature, format, deliverable, language, size or version? | **Change** |
| 3 | Does it reverse or redo something the client already approved? | **Change** |
| 4 | Does it adjust work that's in scope and not yet approved (wording, colour, order, emphasis, tone)? | **Revision** (uses a round) |

If none of these fit, it's usually a change in direction. Treat it as a change, and talk to the client before quoting: a new direction often means the brief needs rewriting.

## Grey areas and how to handle them

- **"It's tiny."** Size doesn't decide it; the test does. But for genuinely tiny changes (under 15 minutes) you can choose to do them as a goodwill gesture. Log them anyway with price 0 and say so: "Happy to include this one at no charge." Then the client knows it was a favour, not a right.
- **"The brief was vague."** If the brief genuinely didn't specify it, it's a revision. Next time, tighten the brief.
- **"Our CEO saw it and hates it."** A new reviewer arriving late is the most common source of change. If the work matches the approved brief, the CEO's new direction is a change.
- **Lots of small revisions at once.** That's still one round, as long as it comes as one list.

## Twelve examples

| Project | Request | Verdict | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Logo design | "Try the blue a bit darker" | Revision | Adjusts in-scope work |
| Logo design | "Can we also get a version for social media profile pictures?" | Change | New format |
| Website build | "The contact button links to the wrong page" | Revision (free) | Your error |
| Website build | "Add a blog section" | Change | New feature |
| Website build | "Move the testimonials above pricing" | Revision | Order of in-scope content |
| Blog article | "Make the intro punchier" | Revision | Tone, in scope |
| Blog article | "Can you also write three social posts from it?" | Change | New deliverable |
| Blog article | "Actually, we want it aimed at managers, not engineers" | Change | New direction, the brief said engineers |
| Video edit | "Swap this clip for the other take" | Revision | In-scope adjustment |
| Video edit | "We need a 30-second cut as well" | Change | New version |
| Report design | "We approved page 4 last week but want to redo the chart" | Change | Reverses approved work |
| Translation | "Can we add the Spanish version?" | Change | New language |

## Write it down

Whatever you decide, write one line in `change-log.csv` or `revision-tracker.csv`. When you invoice, you'll have a record instead of a memory.
files.change-request-form.md:
# Change Request

Copy this into an email or a document. Keep it short: the point is to make saying yes easy. Fill in everything in [brackets].

---

**Change request #[number] for [project name]**
Date: [date]
Requested by: [client name], on [date / in call / by email]

**What you asked for**
[One or two sentences in plain language. Use the client's own words where possible.]

**What I'll do**
- [Specific task 1]
- [Specific task 2]
- [What's included: rounds of revisions on this change, file formats]

**What's not included**
- [Anything they might assume is included but isn't]

**Cost**
[$X] ([fixed price] / [estimated N hours at $Y/hour, billed at actuals up to $Z])

**Effect on the timeline**
[No change to the delivery date.] / [The delivery date moves from [old date] to [new date].] / [This can be done in parallel; the original delivery date stays the same, and this change will be ready on [date].]

**Effect on other work**
[None.] / [Because this adds a new section, the homepage layout will need adjusting too; that's included in the price above.]

**To approve**
Reply "Approved" to this email and I'll start on [date]. If I don't hear back, I'll carry on with the original scope and we can revisit this any time.

---

## Worked example

**Change request #2 for Riverside Dental website**
Date: 12 March
Requested by: Dr. Patel, in our call on 11 March

**What you asked for**
A page where patients can see the clinic's team, with photos and a short bio for each dentist and hygienist.

**What I'll do**
- Design a new "Meet the team" page (desktop and mobile), matching the existing pages
- Add it to the main navigation and footer
- Two rounds of revisions on the new page

**What's not included**
- Photography (you mentioned your team will provide photos)
- Writing the bios (I'll design with placeholder text; please send the final bios by 20 March)

**Cost**
$540 fixed (about 4.5 hours of design work at $90/hour, plus review time and two revision rounds)

**Effect on the timeline**
The final delivery date moves from 28 March to 2 April.

**Effect on other work**
The navigation needs one extra item, which slightly changes the header on every page. That's included in the price above.

**To approve**
Reply "Approved" to this email and I'll start on 14 March. If I don't hear back, I'll carry on with the original five pages and we can add this any time.

---

## Tips

- **Send it the same day.** A change request sent a week later feels like a surprise bill.
- **Always include "effect on the timeline".** Clients care about dates more than money surprisingly often, and it's the part most freelancers leave out.
- **Give them an easy no.** The last line ("If I don't hear back, I'll carry on...") removes pressure and keeps the project moving.
- **Number your requests.** "Change request #3" makes it clear that changes are a normal, tracked part of the project.
- **Never start before the written yes.** A verbal "sounds fine" in a call is not approval. Follow up with the form and wait for the reply.
files.pricing-a-change.md:
# Pricing a Change in Two Minutes

Most freelancers underprice changes because they only count the obvious task. A change also costs you time to understand it, fit it into the schedule, update related work, and review it with the client.

## Fill in your numbers once

| Setting | Your number | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Hourly rate (what you'd charge for the main project, divided by its estimated hours) | [ ] | $90 |
| Minimum change fee (covers assessing, quoting, scheduling) | [ ] | $90 (one hour) |
| Overhead multiplier (for communication, ripple effects, review) | [ ] | 1.3 |
| Rush multiplier (less than [3] working days' notice) | [ ] | 1.5 |
| Round up to nearest | [ ] | $10 |

## The formula

```
Price = max( Minimum fee,  Task hours x Hourly rate x Overhead multiplier [x Rush multiplier] )
```

Then round up.

## Step by step

1. **List the tasks.** Write the change as 2 to 6 concrete tasks. If you can't, ask the client a clarifying question before pricing.
2. **Estimate hours for each task.** Be honest; if you usually overrun, add 20%.
3. **Check for ripple effects.** Does the change touch anything else? A new page changes the navigation. A new section changes the page length. A new audience changes the tone everywhere. Add those tasks.
4. **Multiply.** Hours x rate x overhead.
5. **Apply rush** if the deadline is tight.
6. **Apply the minimum** if the result is below it.
7. **Round up** and write it on the change request.

## Worked example 1: a new page

Sam (designer, $90/hour) is asked to add a "Meet the team" page.

| Task | Hours |
|---|---|
| Design the page layout (desktop) | 2.5 |
| Mobile version | 1.0 |
| Update navigation and footer on all pages | 0.5 |
| Prepare files for the developer | 0.5 |
| **Total** | **4.5** |

4.5 x $90 x 1.3 = $526.50. Round up to **$530**. Sam actually quoted $540, rounding up a little more because the change comes with two revision rounds of its own. Either price is reasonable; what matters is that it covers the ripple effects, not just the page.

## Worked example 2: a small tweak

A writer ($70/hour) is asked to add a short FAQ of five questions to an approved article.

| Task | Hours |
|---|---|
| Draft five Q&As | 0.75 |
| Fit into article, adjust intro | 0.25 |
| **Total** | **1.0** |

1.0 x $70 x 1.3 = $91. Minimum fee is $70, so the formula wins: **$91, round to $95**.

## Worked example 3: a rush change

A video editor ($80/hour) is asked, two days before delivery, to add a 30-second cut.

3 hours x $80 x 1.3 x 1.5 = $468. Round to **$470**. The change request says plainly: "Because this is needed before Friday, it's billed at my rush rate."

## Fixed price or hourly?

- **Fixed price** when you can estimate confidently (most small changes). Clients approve fixed prices faster.
- **Hourly with a cap** when the change is fuzzy: "Estimated 5 to 8 hours at $90/hour, billed at actuals and capped at $720. I'll tell you if it looks like going over."

## When to do it for free

It's your business, so you choose. Some freelancers keep a small goodwill allowance (say, 30 minutes per project) for tiny changes. If you do, still log the change with price 0 and tell the client: "No charge for this one." It keeps the boundary visible.

# Getting One Clear Feedback List Per Round

Scattered feedback (three people, four channels, contradicting each other) is the main reason projects run over. Consolidated feedback is faster for the client too: they make the decisions once instead of you guessing.

## 1. Set it up at kickoff

Agree on three things and write them in your kickoff summary email:

- **The feedback owner:** one named person who sends each round.
- **The channel:** one place feedback arrives (usually email, or one shared document).
- **The deadline:** when feedback for each round is due.

## 2. Send a feedback request with every delivery

Don't just send files with "Let me know what you think." Ask for exactly the feedback you need.

> Hi [name],
>
> Round [1] of [the homepage design] is ready: [link or attachment].
>
> When you're ready, please send your feedback as **one list** by [date]. It helps most if each point says:
> 1. **Where** (page, section or timestamp)
> 2. **What** isn't working
> 3. **Why**, if you know (for example, "patients won't understand this term")
>
> If several people are reviewing, could you combine their notes and settle any disagreements before sending? That way I can turn it around in [3] working days.
>
> This is round [1] of [2].
>
> Thanks,
> [your name]

## 3. Turn their feedback into an action list

When feedback arrives, paste it into a table before you start. This takes 10 minutes and saves hours.

| # | Where | Their comment | What I'll do | Type | Question? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | | | | Revision / Change / Error | |

Send the table back if anything is unclear or if any item is a change:

> Thanks, this is really clear. Here's how I'm reading it, so we're on the same page. Items 1-6 I'll do in this round. Item 7 (adding a booking widget) is new, so I've sent a separate quote for it. One question on item 4: [question]. I'll start as soon as you confirm.

## Worked example

Dr. Patel's team sent feedback in an email, two chat messages and a voice note. Sam consolidated it:

| # | Where | Their comment | What I'll do | Type | Question? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Homepage hero | "Feels cold" | Warmer photo, softer blue | Revision | Do you have clinic photos, or should I use stock? |
| 2 | Homepage hero | "Phone number should be bigger" | Increase size, add tap-to-call on mobile | Revision | |
| 3 | Services | "Missing Invisalign" | Add item to services list | Error (in brief, I missed it) | |
| 4 | Services | "Too much text" (receptionist) vs "Need more detail" (Dr. Patel) | Short summaries with "Learn more" links | Revision | Dr. Patel, does this work for both? |
| 5 | Footer | "Add opening hours" | Add hours block | Revision | |
| 6 | Whole site | "Can we add a team page?" | Separate quote sent | Change | |

Six messy comments became five clear tasks, two questions and one change request.

## When feedback still arrives scattered

- **Late comments after you've started:** "Thanks! I've already started on round 1, so I'll add this to round 2."
- **Contradicting reviewers:** don't choose for them. "I've had two different steers on the services section. Could [owner] let me know which way to go?"
- **Feedback in calls:** summarise it in writing straight after: "Here's what I took from our call. Reply if I've missed anything; otherwise I'll start on this tomorrow."
files.email-scripts.md:
# Ten Emails for the Awkward Moments

Replace everything in [brackets]. Keep the friendly tone: the goal is to protect the project, not to win an argument.

---

## 1. Kickoff: how feedback works

> Subject: How feedback and changes work on [project]
>
> Hi [name],
>
> Really looking forward to this. A quick note on how feedback works, so nothing's ever a surprise:
>
> - You get [two] rounds of revisions on each [deliverable].
> - A round is one combined list of feedback from [feedback owner].
> - If something new comes up that's outside what we agreed, I'll send a short quote first. Nothing extra gets billed without your written OK.
>
> First delivery is on [date]. Any questions, just ask.
>
> [your name]

## 2. "That's a change" (gently)

> Hi [name],
>
> Great idea. Adding [the thing] is outside the original scope, so I've put together a quick change request with the cost and timing: [attached / below].
>
> If you'd like to go ahead, just reply "Approved". If not, no problem at all; I'll carry on with the original plan.

## 3. Last included round

> Hi [name],
>
> Round [2] is attached. Just a heads-up that this is the last included round on [deliverable], so it's worth gathering everyone's final thoughts before sending feedback.
>
> If you need more rounds after this, extra rounds are [$X] each.

## 4. Rounds used up, more feedback arrives

> Hi [name],
>
> Thanks for these notes. We've used the [two] included rounds on [deliverable], so this would be an extra round at [$X]. Happy to go ahead: just reply to confirm, and I'll have it back to you by [date].
>
> If it helps, items [3 and 5] are quick fixes I'm happy to include at no charge.

## 5. Asking for consolidated feedback

> Hi [name],
>
> I've had a few notes come in from different people on [deliverable], and a couple point in different directions. To make sure I build the right thing, could you combine them into one list and settle [the question about X]? I'll start as soon as I have it.

## 6. Verbal approval in a call

> Hi [name],
>
> Thanks for the call. As discussed, I'll add [change] for [$X], and the delivery date moves to [date]. Could you reply "Approved" to confirm? I'll start as soon as I have that in writing.

## 7. Declining a change

> Hi [name],
>
> Thanks for thinking of me for [the thing]. It's not something I can do well [/ fit in before the deadline], so I'd rather not take it on and do it badly. [If you can: I'd suggest looking for a specialist in X.] I'll keep the original plan on track for [date].

## 8. A change that moves the deadline

> Hi [name],
>
> I can definitely add [change]. It's about [N] days of work, so we have two options:
>
> 1. Add it now: the delivery date moves from [date] to [date]. Cost [$X].
> 2. Launch on [original date] as planned, and add it the week after. Same cost.
>
> Which works better for you?

## 9. Reversing an approved decision

> Hi [name],
>
> Understood. Since [deliverable] was approved on [date], reworking it now counts as a change rather than a revision. I've estimated it at [$X] and [N] extra days: [change request]. Happy to go ahead once you confirm.

## 10. Invoice with changes

> Hi [name],
>
> Attached is the invoice for [project]. Alongside the original [$X], it includes the [two] changes you approved:
>
> - Change request #1, [short name], approved [date]: [$X]
> - Change request #2, [short name], approved [date]: [$X]
>
> Total: [$X], due [date]. Thanks again; it's been a great project.
